episodes.182694: Ample residual moisture lingered across west-central Colorado. This led to another round of diurnally-driven showers and thunderstorms, favoring the mountains along the Divide. Some storms produced heavy rain. One such storm produced localized flooding in a portion of Eagle County.
episodes.182700: Isolated strong thunderstorms developed during the midday into the early afternoon hours in northeast Alabama producing gusty winds. Later in the afternoon and early evening, a complex of thunderstorms dropped south from middle Tennessee into north Alabama. A strong gust front surged south of the thunderstorms producing wind damage at a few locations in Colbert County in northwest Alabama.
episodes.182740: A series of training thunderstorms produced extremely high rainfall across portions of Patrick and Carroll Counties during the predawn hours of August 28th. This resulted in areas of flash flooding, mainly in the headwaters of the Smith River and the Ararat River. ||The event began with a stationary front draped near the border of Virginia and North Carolina early on the 28th as an upper level disturbance began passing across the lower Great Lakes, placing the central Appalachians in an area of lift. The disturbance triggered a southeasterly wind shift across the foothills of the Blue Ridge in southern Virginia and northern North Carolina, bringing an increase of deep moisture northeast from the Piedmont of North Carolina. Precipitable water values were estimated to|be 1.9 to 2.1 inches across Patrick and Carroll counties by 3:00 am on the 28th, while Mixed-Layer CAPE values remained around 500 J/Kg through much of the night.||Convection initiated after sunset on the 27th as a few slow-moving showers across southern Patrick County. Coverage and intensity of the slow-moving activity only increased as the evening progressed, with a band of showers and embedded storms forming along the Highway 58 corridor by midnight, that was advancing northeast toward the crest of the Blue Ridge. Deep moisture combined with orographic lift to produce extremely efficient rainfall rates that were, at times, ranging from 3 to 5 inches per hour across Patrick County into neighboring Carroll County. Doppler Radar estimated rainfall totals of nearly 11 inches of rainfall in northern Patrick County across the Smith River basin, which was confirmed by one CoCoRaHS report of 10.70 inches, as well as a Cooperative Observer report from Woolwine of 10.62 inches. The stream gage at the Smith River near Woolwine (SMWV2) rose to 11.04 feet, just above moderate flood stage due to this rainfall, however radar estimates put the highest amounts downstream of this gage.  Few reports of flooding impacts were received, however it was noted that Philpott Reservoir rose 3 feet in response to the inflows from the Smith River. In western Patrick County and southeast Carroll County, 4 to 7 inches of rain fell across the entire headwaters of the Ararat River, with radar estimates of around 9 inches near the town of Ararat, VA. Flash flooding in this area resulted in several roads being destroyed or heavily damaged where they passed over flooded creeks and rivers, including the Ararat River.
episodes.183043: Training thunderstorms impacted northwest Middle Tennessee during the morning hours of August 27, 2023. Repeated rounds of thunderstorms produced heavy rain which combined with the heavy rain from the previous day caused minor street flooding in portions of Stewart County.
episodes.183389: A trough of low pressure across the Midlands was the focus for widely scattered strong to severe thunderstorms. The storms produced strong damaging wind gusts.
episodes.183400: A stalled frontal boundary across the Midlands and Central Savannah River Area was the focus showers and storms that produced locally heavy rainfall and isolated damaging winds.
episodes.183402: A stalled frontal boundary across the Midlands and Central Savannah River Area was the focus showers and storms that produced isolated damaging winds.
episodes.183937: Monsoon moisture brought several pushes of moisture to the region which brought heavy rainfall to most areas, with the daily record in Boise set.
episodes.184049: Scattered thunderstorms developed in the afternoon across North and Central GA. A few storms became severe with localized microbursts causing isolated wind damage.
episodes.184203: A sagging cold front sluggishly pressed through West Virginia beginning on August 25th, continuing to shift eastward on the 26th. The slow nature of this boundary promoted an extended period of showers and thunderstorms spanning both days. ||Starting on the 25th, a few thunderstorms sprouted during the predawn hours through parts of north central West Virginia, with individual tree damage noted in each county. A few storms reached severe levels during the morning rush hour, with strong winds causing additional tree damage in Clay and Kanawha Counties. Within the storms passing over Kanawha County, bursts of heavier rainfall took place, and caused minor high water issues in known trouble areas in and around downtown Charleston. While the bulk of storms diminished shortly after sunrise, another round of flash flooding occurred in parts of Teays Valley in Putnam County and eastward near the Putnam/Kanawha County lines early that morning.||On the next day on August 26th, more rain fell across parts of eastern Kanawha County. The disturbance imposing the slow moving cold front finally set sail to the east on the 26th so convection chances quickly diminished. However, the ground conditions left behind by these two days of precipitation would set the stage for major flash flooding to take shape on August 28th.
episodes.184211: A small thunderstorm complex over the Pennyrile region of western Kentucky slowed down and intensified during the morning. A very well-defined and slow-moving mesoscale convective vortex over southeast Missouri drifted off to the southeast through the morning hours, tracking into western Kentucky by midday. This system interacted with a very moist and modestly unstable air mass, resulting in heavy rainfall and isolated flash flooding. Precipitable water values remained very high, with values of 2.0 to 2.25 inches characteristic of a deeply tropical air mass. One person drowned as a result of floodwaters in west-central Christian County.
episodes.184233: Widespread precipitation fell across the Talkeetna, Susitna, Yentna and Skwenta Basins in late August as a deep, upper-level low anchored itself over the Bering Sea, sending waves of precipitation through the area. The persistent moist pattern followed a prolonged period of wet conditions over the previous months, leading to high flows and flooding across the Susitna Basin and associated rivers in the basin over the course of the period.
episodes.184432: Scattered diurnal convection developed across southern Oklahoma on the evening of the 26th. While wind shear was weak, plentiful instability lead to downburst wind events with the strongest storms. A report of large hail was also received with a briefly organized storm in Murray County, Oklahoma.
episodes.184519: An active weather pattern in August 2023 kept conditions in the Copper River Basin near saturation.  An atmospheric river moved into Prince William Sound August 26 and heavy rains elevated river levels, impacting access to Solomon Gulch Dam and limiting transportation along Richardson Highway.
episodes.184656: A severe thunderstorm produced large hail up to half dollar size.
episodes.184767: Heavy rain caused some minor road flooding.
episodes.184809: Large hail, strong winds and funnel clouds all reported on the 27th.
episodes.184955: Abundant moisture along a slow moving cold front led to the development of scattered thunderstorms the afternoon and evenings of Saturday August 26 and Sunday August 27 as an upper level disturbance moved across the Southern Plains. Minor wind damage occurred in several of these storms, primarily across Central Texas.
episodes.185016: A weak cold front drifted into Central Louisiana during a heat wave. The very hot and unstable airmass ahead of the boundary produced a round of severe weather with high wind gusts and downed trees.
episodes.185018: A weak cold front drifted into the region from the north during a heat wave. Ahead of the boundary isolated thunderstorms developed with two becoming severe.
episodes.185136: A surface trough combined with a moist and unstable air mass resulted in an area of showers and storms moving west from the Appalachians into the northwestern Piedmont during the evening. A couple of trees were reported down from the storms in Davidson County.
episodes.185190: Isolated wind damage occurred with thunderstorms on the afternoons of August 25th and 27th.
episodes.185260: Scattered thunderstorms near a frontal boundary produced heavy rain which caused flash flooding across portions of northeast North Carolina.
episodes.185385: A cluster of thunderstorms moved across the North Carolina Piedmont during mid-to-late evening. Isolated strong-to-damaging wind gusts occurred.
episodes.185386: Scattered thunderstorms and storm clusters developed across western North Carolina throughout the afternoon into the evening. Some storms produced brief damaging wind gusts.
episodes.185387: Scattered thunderstorms and storm clusters developed across northeast Georgia during the afternoon. One of the storms produced brief damaging wind gusts in Franklin County.
episodes.185400: Thunderstorms were observed developing along a nearly stalled frontal boundary and remnant outflows across parts of Southwest Arkansas, Northeast Texas, and Northern Louisiana on the afternoon of August 27th. Very strong diurnal heating was sufficient to erode a capping inversion aloft with around 1500-2000 J/kg of mean-layer instability supporting occasional stronger updrafts. Deep-layer vertical shear across much of the region was weak at generally less than 10-15 knots. This was still enough to support multi-cellular, pulse convection as the primary storm mode. Weak surface flow was also insufficient to support much cold pool propagation. Therefore, the primary severe risk was tied to individual pulse downdrafts as thunderstorms collapsed. This resulted in numerous damaging wind reports across parts of the region, including one isolated report in Little River County.
episodes.185401: Thunderstorms were observed developing along a nearly stalled frontal boundary and remnant outflows across parts of Southwest Arkansas, Northeast Texas, and Northern Louisiana on the afternoon of August 27th. Very strong diurnal heating was sufficient to erode a capping inversion aloft with around 1500-2000 J/kg of mean-layer instability supporting occasional stronger updrafts. Deep-layer vertical shear across much of the region was weak at generally less than 10-15 knots. This was still enough to support multi-cellular, pulse convection as the primary storm mode. Weak surface flow was also insufficient to support much cold pool propagation. Therefore, the primary severe risk was tied to individual pulse downdrafts as thunderstorms collapsed. This resulted in numerous damaging wind reports across parts of the region, including several reports in parts of Caddo Parish and one in Natchitoches Parish.
episodes.185402: Thunderstorms were observed developing along a nearly stalled frontal boundary and remnant outflows across parts of Southwest Arkansas, Northeast Texas, and Northern Louisiana on the afternoon of August 27th. Very strong diurnal heating was sufficient to erode a capping inversion aloft with around 1500-2000 J/kg of mean-layer instability supporting occasional stronger updrafts. Deep-layer vertical shear across much of the region was weak at generally less than 10-15 knots. This was still enough to support multi-cellular, pulse convection as the primary storm mode. Weak surface flow was also insufficient to support much cold pool propagation. Therefore, the primary severe risk was tied to individual pulse downdrafts as thunderstorms collapsed. This resulted in numerous damaging wind reports across parts of the region, including a few isolated reports in Rusk and Harrison County.
episodes.185418: A typical summertime convective regime was in place for the 27th. However, the air was slightly cooler aloft and that helped promote hail in the strongest storms across southeast Louisiana along with a damaging wind threat.
episodes.185419: A typical summertime convective regime was in place for the 27th. However, the air was slightly cooler aloft and that helped promote hail in the strongest storms across southeast Louisiana and the immediate coastal waters along with a damaging wind threat.
episodes.185553: Afternoon and evening sea breeze thunderstorms produce gusty winds across Tampa Bay and neighboring waters as well as Fort Myers area waters.

events.narrative: Relayed image.
A power pole was knocked down or leaning at 555 Allen Lane due to gust front winds. Time estimated by radar.
Dispatchers reported that lightning struck a home on Queen Chapel Road and caused a fire which produced minor damage. Exact monetary value of damage unknown.
A couple of trees were reported down just to the west of Lexington.
Multiple sources reported reported multiple trees and large limbs blown down from Forney Hill Rd to the western shores of Lake Norman, including Unity Church Rd.

A clogged culvert resulted in minor flooding issues of two houses residing along Little Creek Road. Slaughters Creek rose above its banks and caused high water issues along Slaughters Creek Road and Westwood Drive.
County comms reported multiple trees and power lines blown down on Shiloh Church Rd.
Multiple tress and power lines were blown down in the Cornelius area.
County comms reported numerous trees and some power lines  blown down across north Charlotte.

Flood waters encroached on cabins along the Yentna and Skwentna Rivers.  2-4 inches of rain fell within the basin causing river levels to swell, and inundating land areas alongside cabins on the river's edge of the Yentna and Skwentna Rivers.

Heavy rains of 2-4  inches in the Little Susitna Basin, along with much higher rainfall amounts along the mountain headwaters, caused rapid river rises along the Little Susitna River and its tributaries.  High water impacted areas around the Enchanted Forest area of Houston and at campgrounds in Hatcher's Pass.
County comms reported trees and power lines blown down near Cramerton.

Heavy rain across the Talkeetna Mountains caused rapid rises along the Talkeetna River.  1-3 inches of rainfall in the basin, with much higher rainfall amounts in the mountains and headwaters, kept rivers consistently high over a long period of time; this contributed to widespread flooding and areas of bank erosion in Talkeeta.

Heavy rain in Valdez from an atmospheric river, caused Solomon Gulch to flood, closing Dayville Road in Valdez.  This road is the access to the Solomon Gulch Dam and power plant and employees were not able to easily access the plant because the main road was flooded.
The official NWS measurement after a 24 hour period was 2.42 inches of rain.
The mesonet station LLAI1 at Boise measured 2.42 inches of heavy rain.

Heavy rain, on top of saturated soils, caused fast rises on the Lowe River in Valdez.  The Richardson Highway was impacted in Valdez, with flooding encroaching on the highway and closing it at MP 4.  Transportation into/out of Valdez was affected; this is the only road in/out of the community.
A few large tree limbs were blown down in the Rome and Parchman areas, and damage occurred to tin roof on a mobile home.
Several roads were flooded in Princeton.

The Cooperative Weather Observer at Woolwine, VA (WLWV2) measured a 24-hour rainfall total of 10.62 inches, a new all-time record for a 24-hour precipitation total for this station. However, the vast majority of this rainfall fell within a 6-hour window per MRMS data, which would make this total greater than a 1,000-year rainfall event per NOAA Atlas 14 point precipitation frequency estimates.  Runoff from this location flows into the Smith River.

A CoCoRaHS observer (VA-PR-8) measured a 24-hour rainfall total of 10.70 inches. However, the vast majority of this rainfall fell within a 6-hour window per MRMS data, which would make this total greater than a 1,000-year rainfall event per NOAA Atlas 14 point precipitation frequency estimates. Runoff from this location flows into the Smith River.

A CoCoRaHS observer (VA-PR-1) measured a 24-hour rainfall total of 6.30 inches. However, the vast majority of this rainfall fell within a 6-hour window per MRMS data, which would make this total between a 50-year and a 100-year rainfall event per NOAA Atlas 14 point precipitation frequency estimates.

Training thunderstorms near Bumpus Mills during the morning hours produced heavy rain. This combined with the rainfall from the previous day caused minor street flooding in the area. A CoCoRaHS observer reported 2.56 inches of rain within one hour which filled the ditches and caused street flooding.

Numerous roads were flooded throughout the county. Water was over a number of state roads, including Kentucky Routes 1453, 115, 1026, 1663, 1386, 164, and 272. A vehicle carrying five occupants (4 juveniles and an adult female) went into chest high water near the intersection of Buffalo Rd and Gracey Sinking Fork Rd. A rescue operation was performed, removing all of the occupants from the vehicle. The 68-year-old female driver was found to have died as a result of drowning.

A personal weather station (Weather Underground: KVAHILLS12) recorded a 24 hour rainfall amount, ending at 11 am EST on the 28th, of 6.91 inches.  This 24-hour total is between a 10-year and a 25-year Average Recurrence Interval event per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Precipitation Frequency estimates.

A personal weather station (Weather Underground: KVAFANCY19) recorded a 24 hour rainfall amount, ending at 11 am EST on the 28th, of 6.19 inches.  This 24-hour total is between a 10-year and a 25-year Average Recurrence Interval event per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Precipitation Frequency estimates.
A personal weather station (Weather Underground: KVAPATRI8) recorded a 24 hour rainfall amount, ending at 11 am EST on the 28th, of 6.08 inches.
A personal weather station (Weather Underground: KVADOBYN2) recorded a 24 hour rainfall amount, ending at 11 am EST on the 28th, of 5.90 inches.
Water was over roadways in Guthrie and Trenton.
Public report of a tree down and some roof damage to an apartment complex near 27th St.
Public report of a tree down near the intersection of Veterans Pkwy and River Rd.
KCSG reported a wind gust of 64 mph.

One to three inches of heavy rainfall flooded low lying areas of the Susitna Valley, including the main road that crossed Kroto and Moose Creeks.  This road closure limited resident access to their homes.
AWOS station KHDC Hammond recorded a wind gust of 59 mph or 51 knots.

Public report via social media of a tree down across Collins Hill Rd near Radner Run.

A large tree downed near the intersection of County Road 3206 and County Road 3155 just west of Mount Enterprise.
